screens.title: The Hack Computer Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Today we study the Hack computer, a deliberately minimal yet complete machine that demonstrates how a real computer works. You will learn the programmer-visible registers, how memory is arranged for data and input and output, and the two 16-bit instruction formats that let the C P U compute and control program flow. We will treat the A register not just as a number holder but also as an address pointer, and we will see how the shorthand M represents the R A M cell addressed by A. You will learn how the ALU is driven by the comp bits, how dest bits choose where results go, and how the three-bit jump field uses the ALU’s zero and negative flags to implement conditional branching. Understanding these elements matters because they show how software maps to hardware — a small set of bits carries both data and control. For a concrete orientation, we will translate a short assembly example that adds two constants and stores the result in R A M. By the end, you should be able to read Hack machine code and trace simple programs, and you’ll see why the design chooses minimality over convenience.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › The Hack Computer Architecture
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

The Hack Computer Architecture

Explore a purposely minimal computer: two programmer-visible registers, a small ALU, a clear memory map with memory-mapped I/O, and two 16-bit instruction formats that encode data and control.

In this lesson
Registers, memory map, and instruction format
You will trace code, translate assembly to machine code, and reason about jumps using ALU flags.
Why it matters
Minimal hardware reveals core design trade-offs
Fewer registers means a simpler CPU but more careful programming.
Coming up
Example: add two constants and write to RAM
We will translate the assembly to binary and run a mental trace of the PC and registers.
Explore Key Topics
Registers and ALU
How A, D, and the ALU work together to compute and select results.
Memory map
RAM ranges, ROM for instructions, and memory-mapped screen and keyboard.
Instruction formats
A-instruction for addresses/values and C-instruction for computation, destinations, and jumps.
Visual concept
A register
Holds address or value (16 bits)
D register
Dedicated data register used by the ALU for computations.
M = RAM[A]
A convenient shorthand meaning: the memory word located at the address stored in A.
This simplified model shows how a reduced set of registers and a predictable memory map make machine-level behavior easier to reason about while teaching the same principles used in larger architectures.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the Hack architecture precisely, including its programmer-visible registers, the memory map, and how instructions look at the bit level. You will explain the A register’s dual role as data and address, and how the shorthand M refers to R A M at A. You will trace how the ALU comp bits produce computations and how dest bits store ALU outputs into A, D, or memory. You will also analyze jump behavior by interpreting the three jump bits together with the ALU’s zero and negative flags. Practically, you will translate short assembly programs into 16-bit machine code and then mentally execute them using the program counter and register updates. These skills matter because they let you connect high-level program logic to the hardware actions that implement it. For example, when you translate a conditional branch, you will recognize how a comparison reduces to the ALU’s zr and ng flags and how the C P U conditionally loads the PC from A. This combination of description, translation, and tracing is the competency we expect.

screens.title: Programmer-visible registers: A, D, and M
screens.narratorSegment: The Hack C P U exposes two programmer-visible registers and a convenient shorthand for memory: A, D, and M. The A register is a 16-bit value used either as a plain data value or as an address pointer into data memory. The D register is a 16-bit data register used for arithmetic and logical operations. M is not a physical C P U register; it is shorthand that means the memory word found at R A M[A]. In practice this means a single symbol, M, represents an indirection: change A and M refers to a different R A M cell. For example, the assembly sequence @5 followed by D=A loads the number five into D. If instead you want the memory at address 5, you would @5 then use M to read or write R A M[5]. A common mistake is assuming A still holds a useful data value after using it as an address; in many sequences the programmer must save A in D before overwriting A with a new address. The design trade-off is explicit: by sharing A as a value and an address the hardware is simpler, but the programmer must manage the register carefully. As practice, imagine swapping a value: you will typically move a value into D, change A to the target address, and then write D into M. What question do you have about when to save A versus when to treat it as temporary data?

keyIdea.title: Register roles
keyIdea.text: A holds either an address or a value; D stores computation data; M means RAM at address A and is accessed via the A register.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Programmer-visible registers
Definition

A, D, and M explained

A is a 16-bit register used for addresses or values. D is a 16-bit data register for arithmetic. M stands for the memory cell at address A, i.e., RAM[A].

A register
Address or immediate value, 16 bits.
D register
Data workspace for ALU operations.
M (RAM[A])
Shorthand: the memory cell pointed to by A.
Common mistake

Treating A as persistent data after using it to point at memory. Save A to D when you must keep its value across an address change.

Example
// Load 5 into A, copy to D, then store D into RAM[0]
@5      // A = 5
D=A     // D = 5
@0      // A = 0
M=D     // RAM[0] = 5
Why it matters

This small set of registers makes the hardware simple and teaches how software must manage limited state explicitly.

Key Takeaway

Use A when you need an address. Use D to save values across address changes. M reads or writes RAM at A.

screens.title: The A-instruction: loading addresses and values
screens.narratorSegment: The A-instruction is the simplest machine instruction in Hack: its top bit is zero and the remaining fifteen bits form a 15-bit value which is loaded into the A register. Conceptually the instruction looks like a short immediate load: after executing an A-instruction, A contains the provided value. That value can be used directly as data or as a pointer to memory. For example, the assembly @3 becomes a single 16-bit word beginning with zero and ending with the binary representation of three. The loader into A is immediate and does not affect D or PC except that PC advances to the next instruction. A common use pattern is: load an address with @X, then use M to read or write R A M[X], or use D=A to copy that address into D as a value. The minimal instruction design means there is no separate opcode field; the high-order bit distinguishes A-instructions from C-instructions. A misconception to watch for is assuming A-instruction changes memory — it only changes A. To write memory you need a C-instruction that sets M as a destination. Practice by encoding @5 and confirming the fifteen low bits equal the binary for 5. How would you describe the difference between loading an address and writing memory?

keyIdea.title: A-instruction form
keyIdea.text: A-instruction: 0 followed by a 15-bit value; it loads that value into the A register without changing memory directly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › A-instruction
Format

0vvvvvvvvvvvvvvv

The leading 0 bit marks an A-instruction. The remaining 15 bits form the value loaded into A. This is an immediate load.

Example encoding
// @5 becomes: 0 00000000000101
0000000000000101
Misconception

An A-instruction does not write to RAM. It only changes A. Memory writes require a C-instruction that sets M as a destination.

Practical pattern

Common sequence: use @address to set A, then use a C-instruction to read or write M or to compute using A and D. For example, @10; D=M reads RAM[10] into D.

Check your understanding
  • Does @X change RAM? No, it sets A only.
  • How do you write a value into RAM[A]? Use a C-instruction with dest including M.
Key Takeaway

A-instructions load an immediate 15-bit value into A. Use C-instructions to move values from registers into memory.

screens.title: The C-instruction and the ALU comp field
screens.narratorSegment: C-instructions perform computation and control where results go. They begin with three one bits, followed by the a bit, six comp bits, three dest bits, and three jump bits. The comp field encodes what the ALU computes. The a bit selects whether the ALU’s second input is A or M. Together the a and comp bits map to the ALU control signals (named zx, nx, zy, ny, f, no in the Hack ALU design). For example, comp that yields D+A will set control bits to route D and A into the adder path; comp that yields D&M will route inputs into the bitwise and path. A concrete example: the assembly instruction D=D+A is represented by a C-instruction whose comp bits encode the add operation and whose dest bits set D. A frequent confusion is thinking the comp field directly names a high-level operation; instead it encodes a pattern of ALU control flags that implement arithmetic and bitwise primitives. The a bit is crucial: when a is zero the ALU reads the A register; when one it reads M, i. e., R A M[A]. That means identical comp bits perform different computations depending on whether you use A or M. Which operation will you try to encode by hand first: D+A or D&M?

keyIdea.title: Comp field role
keyIdea.text: The comp field, together with the a bit, instructs the ALU what computation to perform by selecting ALU control signals.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › C-instruction: comp field
Format reminder

111 a cccccc ddd jjj

The leading triple ones mark a C-instruction. The a bit selects A versus M for the ALU input. The comp bits choose the operation.

a = 0
ALU uses A as second input.
a = 1
ALU uses M (RAM[A]) as second input.
Pro tip

When you encode arithmetic by hand, first pick the desired operation, then find the comp bits and set a accordingly. Keep a clear list of comp patterns.

Example operations
  • D+A — add D and A (a=0, comp bits for add)
  • D-M — subtract M from D (a=1, comp bits for subtract)
  • !D — bitwise not of D (comp bits for not)
Check
Remember: same comp bits with different a bit mean the ALU uses a different source for the second operand.
Key Takeaway

C-instructions encode both what the ALU computes and which operand to use via the a and comp bits. Learn the comp table to hand-encode operations reliably.

screens.title: Destinations and storing ALU results
screens.narratorSegment: After the ALU computes a value, the C-instruction’s dest bits determine where that result goes. There are three dest bits corresponding to A, D, and M. Any combination is allowed, so a C-instruction can write the same result into multiple places simultaneously. For example, if dest encodes D and M, the ALU output is stored in the D register and in R A M at address A. If dest encodes only A, the result replaces the A register and thus changes which memory cell M will later refer to. A useful pattern is storing a computed pointer and a value simultaneously: AMD=D+A stores the ALU output in all three. A common pitfall occurs when a student expects M to be available at the same cycle if A has been overwritten in the same instruction; remember the ALU computes and then stores simultaneously according to dest bits. Practically, this design keeps the instruction format small and expressive. When you write code by hand, pick dest bits deliberately: use D to save values for further computation, A to set addresses, and M to persist results into memory. What combination of dest bits would you use to both update R A M and keep the value in a register for immediate use?

keyIdea.title: Destinations
keyIdea.text: Dest bits control which of A, D, and M receive the ALU output; combinations allow simultaneous writes to registers and memory.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Destinations and stores
Dest bits

Which targets receive the ALU output?

Three bits correspond to A, D, and M. Any combination can be selected to store the ALU result into those targets in a single instruction.

A
Overwrite A (changes pointer).
D
Save value for future ALU use.
M
Write RAM[A] with ALU output.
Pitfall

Overwriting A and expecting the old A to be used simultaneously. The ALU output is computed, then stored according to the dest bits in that cycle; plan writes accordingly.

Example combinations
  • DEST=010 — write to D only.
  • DEST=001 — write to M only (store to RAM[A]).
  • DEST=111 — write to A, D, and M simultaneously.
Scenario

If you need to compute an address and persist the value while keeping it in D for more math, choose dest bits to write both D and M, or AMD to mirror results.

Key Takeaway

Dest bits give you flexible storage: pick which of A, D, and M should receive the ALU result in a single, compact instruction.

screens.title: The Hack memory map
screens.narratorSegment: The Hack memory map divides address space into clear regions for program and data. Data memory is 16K words, addresses 0 through 16383. The first sixteen words R A M[0..15] are pre-defined symbols R0 through R15. R A M[16..255] holds general static variables. R A M[256..2047] is the stack region used by the VM and compiler, while R A M[2048..16383] is the heap used for objects. The screen is memory-mapped to addresses 16384 through 24575: writing to those words sets pixels on the 256 by 512 monochrome display. Each 16-bit word maps to 16 pixels in a row; there are 32 words per row and 256 rows. The keyboard is a single memory location at address 24576 that contains the ASCII code of the currently pressed key. Instruction memory, ROM, is separate and holds 32K words at addresses 0 through 32767; the C P U fetches from ROM but cannot write to it. A frequent misunderstanding is thinking ROM and R A M overlap: they share address numbering conceptually for the C P U, but ROM holds instructions loaded before execution and is read-only during runtime. Knowing exact ranges matters when you build programs that write to the screen or read keyboard input directly from memory.

keyIdea.text: RAM is 16K with reserved ranges; screen and keyboard are memory-mapped at fixed addresses; ROM stores the program and is read-only.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Memory Map
Hierarchy

RAM and special regions

  • RAM[0..15]: predefined R0..R15
  • RAM[16..255]: general-purpose variables
  • RAM[256..2047]: stack
  • RAM[2048..16383]: heap
Why this matters

Knowing these ranges helps you place variables correctly and avoid corrupting the stack or heap when writing low-level code.

Screen & Keyboard

I/O as memory

Screen: addresses 16384–24575 (8K words) map to a 256×512 bitmap. Keyboard: address 24576 holds the ASCII code of the pressed key.
Screen calculation
256 rows × 32 words/row × 16 bits/word = 8,192 words covering 256×512 bits.
Misconception

Don’t assume writing to screen memory changes ROM; ROM remains read-only. Screen writes are plain RAM stores in the reserved range.

screens.title: ROM, PC, and program flow
screens.narratorSegment: Instruction memory is the ROM region that holds the program: 32K words at addresses 0 through 32767. The C P U fetches instructions from ROM using the program counter (PC), which holds the address of the next instruction to execute. The PC is an internal register not directly visible to Hack assembly code, except through jump behavior: if a C-instruction’s jump condition is true, the PC is loaded with the value in the A register and execution continues from that address. The ROM is read-only at runtime — the simulator or loader places the program into ROM before execution. This design cleanly separates code and writable data memory, making it easier to reason about where programs live and how they are fetched. A misconception students often have is confusing PC updates: most instructions simply increment PC by one; only a jump instruction replaces PC with A. Also remember that the ALU sets two flags we use for jumps: zr indicates the ALU output was zero and ng indicates it was negative. Those flags let the small jump field encode conditions like greater-than or equal. When you trace a program, always update PC, then fetch the instruction at the new PC, unless the current instruction changed PC directly.

keyIdea.title: Program counter and ROM
keyIdea.text: ROM holds instructions; PC selects the next instruction. Jumps load PC from A when the jump condition is true.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › ROM and PC
Instruction memory

ROM: 32K words

ROM holds the program code at addresses 0..32767. The CPU fetches instructions from ROM using the program counter.

Program Counter (PC)
PC contains the ROM address of the next instruction. Normal flow increments PC; jumps load PC from A.
Flags used for jumps

The ALU sets zr and ng flags. The jump field uses these flags to decide whether to load PC from A.

Example flow
  1. Fetch instruction at ROM[PC].
  2. Decode and execute it.
  3. If a jump condition holds, PC := A; otherwise PC := PC + 1.
Check

Only C-instructions with jump bits set can change PC directly. A-instructions simply set A.

Key Takeaway

PC and ROM implement program sequencing; jumps change PC by loading it from A when the ALU flags meet the jump condition.

screens.title: A-instruction vs C-instruction
screens.narratorSegment: Hack machine language uses exactly two 16-bit instruction formats. The A-instruction begins with a single zero and then fifteen bits containing a value. Its sole purpose is to load that value into the A register. The C-instruction begins with three ones followed by a, comp, dest, and jump fields that together perform computation, store results, and optionally change control flow. The distinction is binary and immediate: the very first bit tells the C P U which format to decode. This simplicity makes parsing trivial. To compare concretely: @5 encodes as 0 followed by the 15-bit binary for five; it does not alter memory. A C-instruction like D=D+A becomes a 16-bit word starting with 111, with a selecting A as input, comp bits encoding the add, dest bits indicating D, and jump bits set to no-jump. A common confusion is assuming a C-instruction must include a jump; in fact jump bits can be all zeros for no jump. The compact dual-format design is deliberate: it separates immediate address loads from compute-and-store operations so assembly maps cleanly to machine words. Try encoding both types by hand to internalize the bit patterns.

keyIdea.title: Two formats
keyIdea.text: A-instruction: 0 + 15-bit value. C-instruction: 111 + a + comp + dest + jump; distinguishes compute and control.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › A vs C instructions
A-instruction

0 followed by 15-bit value

Used to load a value into A. Example: @3 → 0000000000000011.

Behavior
Sets A to the given value. Does not change D or write memory by itself.
Check

Can you write the 16-bit word for @10? Convert 10 to 15-bit binary and prefix a zero.

C-instruction

111 a cccccc ddd jjj

Performs computation, writes results, and optionally jumps. The fields control ALU inputs, outputs, and branching.

Example

D=D+A → 111 a comp dest jump with a=0, comp bits for add, dest set for D, jump=000.

Misconception

Not every C-instruction performs a jump. Jump bits can be all zeros meaning no jump; dest bits control storage separately.

screens.title: Jump field and ALU flags
screens.narratorSegment: The C-instruction’s three jump bits encode up to eight jump conditions that the C P U can test after computing an ALU result. The ALU provides two status flags: zr, which is true when the output equals zero, and ng, true when the output is negative. Using these two flags plus the three-bit jump field, the C P U implements conditions like JGT, JEQ, JGE, JLT, JNE, JLE, JMP, and no jump. For instance, JEQ fires when zr is true; JGT fires when neither zr nor ng is true, which indicates a positive result. JGE fires when not ng, covering zero or positive. JLE uses ng or zr to capture negative or zero. JMP unconditionally loads PC from A. The implementation is small: a combinational circuit checks the jump bits against zr and ng and produces a signal to load the PC. A misconception is thinking the ALU must perform separate compare instructions; in Hack, every ALU operation naturally yields zr and ng as side effects, and the jump logic reuses them. When writing assembly, pick the comp that produces the value to be tested, then set the jump bits to the condition you want. How would you implement a 'jump if not equal' using the ALU flags?

keyIdea.title: Jump logic
keyIdea.text: Jump bits combine with ALU flags zr and ng to decide whether the PC should be loaded from A, allowing conditional branching with minimal hardware.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Jump field and flags
ALU flags

zr and ng

zr is true when ALU output equals zero. ng is true when the output is negative. Positive is represented by neither flag set.

JEQ → zr
JGT → not ng and not zr
JGE → not ng
JLT → ng
JNE → not zr
JLE → ng or zr
JMP → unconditional
Implementation note

A small combinational logic block maps the three jump bits and the two flags to a PC-load signal. No extra comparator hardware is required.

Example

To jump when two values are unequal, compute their difference in the ALU and set jump bits for JNE. If the result is nonzero, zr will be false and JNE triggers because it is the "not zero" condition.

Check

When encoding jumps, always choose a comp that produces a value whose sign or zero-ness matches the condition you want to test.

Key Takeaway

Two ALU flags plus three jump bits let the machine express seven conditional jumps and no-jump with very little hardware.

screens.title: Walkthrough: add 2 and 3, store result in RAM[0]
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s walk through a concrete program that adds 2 and 3 and stores the sum in R A M[0]. The assembly uses six instructions that load constants and perform computation. We start with @2 which sets A to two. Next D=A copies that value into D. Then @3 sets A to three. D=D+A instructs the ALU to add D and A, placing five into D. Then @0 sets A to zero, and M=D stores D into R A M[0]. Translating these to machine code: @2 becomes 0 followed by 15-bit binary for 2. D=A is a C-instruction that sets dest to D and comp to A, similarly encoded. When you manually translate, produce each 16-bit word and verify that the A-instructions start with 0. During execution trace the registers: after @2 and D=A D holds 2. After @3 and D=D+A D holds 5. After @0 and M=D R A M[0] holds 5. A useful check is to ensure you didn’t accidentally overwrite D when changing A. Also confirm that only the C-instruction M=D writes to R A M. This example reveals how a few instructions manipulate A, D, and memory to perform simple arithmetic and storage.

keyIdea.title: Example program
keyIdea.text: A short sequence of A- and C-instructions loads constants, computes with the ALU, and writes a result to RAM[0]; tracing registers confirms each step.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Example: add 2 + 3
Assembly
// Add 2 + 3 and store the result in RAM[0]
@2      // A = 2
D=A     // D = A (D = 2)
@3      // A = 3
D=D+A   // D = D + A (D = 5)
@0      // A = 0
M=D     // RAM[0] = D (RAM[0] = 5)
Machine words (example encoding)
0000000000000010  // @2
1110110000010000  // D=A  (example comp/dest/jump bits)
0000000000000011  // @3
1110000010010000  // D=D+A
0000000000000000  // @0
1110001100001000  // M=D
Trace
  • After D=A: D = 2, A = 2.
  • After @3 and D=D+A: D = 5, A = 3.
  • After @0 and M=D: RAM[0] = 5.
Concrete check

Confirm each A-instruction binary begins with 0 and C-instructions begin with 111. Verify only M=D writes to RAM.

Reflection

This simple program demonstrates how immediate loads and ALU operations combine to compute and persist a result to memory.

screens.title: Practice exercises: swap, countdown, and find max
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter suggests three hands-on programs to solidify your understanding: swapping two values using a temporary, a countdown that stores intermediate values, and finding the maximum of two values using conditional jumps. For swap, the plan is simple: load R A M[0] into D, store D into R A M[2] as temporary, load R A M[1] into D, write it to R A M[0], then restore R A M[1] from R A M[2]. For countdown, initialize R A M[0] with 10, then loop: store the current value into the next R A M slot, decrement the counter, and jump when not zero. This exercise trains stack-like memory usage and loop control using jump bits. For find max, load R A M[0] and R A M[1], compute their difference into the ALU, and use jump bits to decide which value to store into R A M[2]. Each program requires you to produce both assembly and the corresponding 16-bit binary words. When translating by hand, encode each A-instruction as 0+value and encode each C-instruction by selecting a, comp, dest, and jump fields. A common debugging approach is to step through the PC and record A, D, and R A M snapshots after each instruction to confirm correctness. These exercises force you to manage A carefully, choose dest bits, and use jumps. Which program will you implement first?

keyIdea.title: Practice plan
keyIdea.text: Write assembly for swap, countdown, and find-max; hand-encode each instruction to 16-bit machine words and trace registers and RAM for verification.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Hands-on Activity
Swap two values

Use RAM[2] as temporary storage. Steps: D=M (with A=0), @2; M=D, then load RAM[1] and write to RAM[0], finally restore RAM[1] from RAM[2]. Translate each step to machine words and verify.

Countdown

Initialize RAM[0]=10. Loop: write counter to RAM[i], decrement counter, increment i, and branch until zero. Implement loop control with jumps based on ALU flags.

Find max

Load RAM[0] and RAM[1], compute difference, and use a conditional jump to choose which value to store into RAM[2]. Translate each instruction to bits and simulate PC, A, D updates.

Verification strategy

Step through each instruction and record A, D, and RAM snapshots. Confirm A-instructions begin with 0 and that only C-instructions with M in dest write to RAM. Hand-encoding and tracing are the fastest path to finding mistakes.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the core ideas to take with you. First, the programmer-visible registers are A and D; M is a shorthand for R A M[A], so A plays a dual role as value and address. Second, the memory map divides writable R A M (0–16383), a memory-mapped screen (16384–24575), and the keyboard at 24576. Third, instruction memory (ROM) is separate and read-only; the PC steps through ROM and jumps load PC from A. Fourth, there are exactly two instruction formats: A-instructions load A with a 15-bit value and begin with 0; C-instructions begin with 111 and include a, comp, dest, and jump fields. Fifth, comp bits drive the ALU, and dest bits choose where the ALU output is stored. Sixth, jump bits use the ALU’s zr and ng flags to express conditional branching. These compact mechanisms show how a small instruction set and a minimal register file can still express useful computation and control flow. Keep these relationships in mind when translating assembly to binary and when tracing programs.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts
Registers (A, D, M)
A holds an address or value; D is the data register; M denotes RAM[A].
Memory map
RAM 0–16383; screen 16384–24575; keyboard 24576; ROM holds instructions.
Instruction formats
A: 0 + 15-bit value. C: 111 + a + comp + dest + jump.
Summary takeaway

The Hack architecture uses a minimal set of registers and compact instruction fields to teach the mapping from bits to computation and control. Master the small tables and practice hand-encoding to internalize the model.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three compact reminders handy. First: A is address-or-value, D is the data workspace, and M always means R A M[A]. Second: A-instructions start with 0 and load A with a 15-bit immediate; C-instructions start with 111 and encode computation, destinations, and optional jumps. Third: Jumps are implemented by the three jump bits combined with the ALU flags zr and ng; no separate comparator hardware is needed. These three reminders let you spot encoding errors, reason about loops, and predict the effect of each instruction on registers and memory. When you hand-encode and trace programs, start by deciding whether an instruction is an A- or C-instruction, then fill in comp, dest, and jump for C-instructions, or write the immediate bits for A-instructions. That small workflow will make translating and debugging predictable and fast.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Quick Reference
A vs C
A: 0+value. C: 111 + fields. Decide format first when encoding.
Registers reminder
A holds address/value. D is data. M = RAM[A]. Save A to D if you need it later.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we study the Hack computer, a deliberately minimal yet complete machine that demonstrates how a real computer works. You will learn the programmer-visible registers, how memory is arranged for data and input and output, and the two 16-bit instruction formats that let the C P U compute and control program flow. We will treat the A register not just as a number holder but also as an address pointer, and we will see how the shorthand M represents the R A M cell addressed by A. You will learn how the ALU is driven by the comp bits, how dest bits choose where results go, and how the three-bit jump field uses the ALU’s zero and negative flags to implement conditional branching. Understanding these elements matters because they show how software maps to hardware — a small set of bits carries both data and control. For a concrete orientation, we will translate a short assembly example that adds two constants and stores the result in R A M. By the end, you should be able to read Hack machine code and trace simple programs, and you’ll see why the design chooses minimality over convenience.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the Hack architecture precisely, including its programmer-visible registers, the memory map, and how instructions look at the bit level. You will explain the A register’s dual role as data and address, and how the shorthand M refers to R A M at A. You will trace how the ALU comp bits produce computations and how dest bits store ALU outputs into A, D, or memory. You will also analyze jump behavior by interpreting the three jump bits together with the ALU’s zero and negative flags. Practically, you will translate short assembly programs into 16-bit machine code and then mentally execute them using the program counter and register updates. These skills matter because they let you connect high-level program logic to the hardware actions that implement it. For example, when you translate a conditional branch, you will recognize how a comparison reduces to the ALU’s zr and ng flags and how the C P U conditionally loads the PC from A. This combination of description, translation, and tracing is the competency we expect.

This screen expands the objectives with concrete checks and examples so you can validate your skill. For the register objective, practice by converting an assembly sequence of A and D instructions into resulting values for A, D, and R A M. For the memory map objective, draw or list the R A M ranges and explain which addresses map to the screen and to the keyboard. For instruction formats, translate both an A-instruction like at-five and a C-instruction such as D equals D plus A to the 16-bit binary representation, checking the a, comp, dest, and jump fields. For tracing, step through a short program with a program counter and update PC, A, D, and the R A M cell referenced by M. Each card gives an explicit milestone: being able to show register contents after three instructions, to list screen and keyboard addresses from memory, to hand-encode two instructions, and to step through a conditional branch. These activities connect description to action and prepare you for the hands-on assembly exercises later in the chapter.

The Hack C P U exposes two programmer-visible registers and a convenient shorthand for memory: A, D, and M. The A register is a 16-bit value used either as a plain data value or as an address pointer into data memory. The D register is a 16-bit data register used for arithmetic and logical operations. M is not a physical C P U register; it is shorthand that means the memory word found at R A M[A]. In practice this means a single symbol, M, represents an indirection: change A and M refers to a different R A M cell. For example, the assembly sequence @5 followed by D=A loads the number five into D. If instead you want the memory at address 5, you would @5 then use M to read or write R A M[5]. A common mistake is assuming A still holds a useful data value after using it as an address; in many sequences the programmer must save A in D before overwriting A with a new address. The design trade-off is explicit: by sharing A as a value and an address the hardware is simpler, but the programmer must manage the register carefully. As practice, imagine swapping a value: you will typically move a value into D, change A to the target address, and then write D into M. What question do you have about when to save A versus when to treat it as temporary data?

The A-instruction is the simplest machine instruction in Hack: its top bit is zero and the remaining fifteen bits form a 15-bit value which is loaded into the A register. Conceptually the instruction looks like a short immediate load: after executing an A-instruction, A contains the provided value. That value can be used directly as data or as a pointer to memory. For example, the assembly @3 becomes a single 16-bit word beginning with zero and ending with the binary representation of three. The loader into A is immediate and does not affect D or PC except that PC advances to the next instruction. A common use pattern is: load an address with @X, then use M to read or write R A M[X], or use D=A to copy that address into D as a value. The minimal instruction design means there is no separate opcode field; the high-order bit distinguishes A-instructions from C-instructions. A misconception to watch for is assuming A-instruction changes memory — it only changes A. To write memory you need a C-instruction that sets M as a destination. Practice by encoding @5 and confirming the fifteen low bits equal the binary for 5. How would you describe the difference between loading an address and writing memory?

C-instructions perform computation and control where results go. They begin with three one bits, followed by the a bit, six comp bits, three dest bits, and three jump bits. The comp field encodes what the ALU computes. The a bit selects whether the ALU’s second input is A or M. Together the a and comp bits map to the ALU control signals (named zx, nx, zy, ny, f, no in the Hack ALU design). For example, comp that yields D+A will set control bits to route D and A into the adder path; comp that yields D&M will route inputs into the bitwise and path. A concrete example: the assembly instruction D=D+A is represented by a C-instruction whose comp bits encode the add operation and whose dest bits set D. A frequent confusion is thinking the comp field directly names a high-level operation; instead it encodes a pattern of ALU control flags that implement arithmetic and bitwise primitives. The a bit is crucial: when a is zero the ALU reads the A register; when one it reads M, i. e., R A M[A]. That means identical comp bits perform different computations depending on whether you use A or M. Which operation will you try to encode by hand first: D+A or D&M?

After the ALU computes a value, the C-instruction’s dest bits determine where that result goes. There are three dest bits corresponding to A, D, and M. Any combination is allowed, so a C-instruction can write the same result into multiple places simultaneously. For example, if dest encodes D and M, the ALU output is stored in the D register and in R A M at address A. If dest encodes only A, the result replaces the A register and thus changes which memory cell M will later refer to. A useful pattern is storing a computed pointer and a value simultaneously: AMD=D+A stores the ALU output in all three. A common pitfall occurs when a student expects M to be available at the same cycle if A has been overwritten in the same instruction; remember the ALU computes and then stores simultaneously according to dest bits. Practically, this design keeps the instruction format small and expressive. When you write code by hand, pick dest bits deliberately: use D to save values for further computation, A to set addresses, and M to persist results into memory. What combination of dest bits would you use to both update R A M and keep the value in a register for immediate use?

The Hack memory map divides address space into clear regions for program and data. Data memory is 16K words, addresses 0 through 16383. The first sixteen words R A M[0..15] are pre-defined symbols R0 through R15. R A M[16..255] holds general static variables. R A M[256..2047] is the stack region used by the VM and compiler, while R A M[2048..16383] is the heap used for objects. The screen is memory-mapped to addresses 16384 through 24575: writing to those words sets pixels on the 256 by 512 monochrome display. Each 16-bit word maps to 16 pixels in a row; there are 32 words per row and 256 rows. The keyboard is a single memory location at address 24576 that contains the ASCII code of the currently pressed key. Instruction memory, ROM, is separate and holds 32K words at addresses 0 through 32767; the C P U fetches from ROM but cannot write to it. A frequent misunderstanding is thinking ROM and R A M overlap: they share address numbering conceptually for the C P U, but ROM holds instructions loaded before execution and is read-only during runtime. Knowing exact ranges matters when you build programs that write to the screen or read keyboard input directly from memory.

Instruction memory is the ROM region that holds the program: 32K words at addresses 0 through 32767. The C P U fetches instructions from ROM using the program counter (PC), which holds the address of the next instruction to execute. The PC is an internal register not directly visible to Hack assembly code, except through jump behavior: if a C-instruction’s jump condition is true, the PC is loaded with the value in the A register and execution continues from that address. The ROM is read-only at runtime — the simulator or loader places the program into ROM before execution. This design cleanly separates code and writable data memory, making it easier to reason about where programs live and how they are fetched. A misconception students often have is confusing PC updates: most instructions simply increment PC by one; only a jump instruction replaces PC with A. Also remember that the ALU sets two flags we use for jumps: zr indicates the ALU output was zero and ng indicates it was negative. Those flags let the small jump field encode conditions like greater-than or equal. When you trace a program, always update PC, then fetch the instruction at the new PC, unless the current instruction changed PC directly.

Hack machine language uses exactly two 16-bit instruction formats. The A-instruction begins with a single zero and then fifteen bits containing a value. Its sole purpose is to load that value into the A register. The C-instruction begins with three ones followed by a, comp, dest, and jump fields that together perform computation, store results, and optionally change control flow. The distinction is binary and immediate: the very first bit tells the C P U which format to decode. This simplicity makes parsing trivial. To compare concretely: @5 encodes as 0 followed by the 15-bit binary for five; it does not alter memory. A C-instruction like D=D+A becomes a 16-bit word starting with 111, with a selecting A as input, comp bits encoding the add, dest bits indicating D, and jump bits set to no-jump. A common confusion is assuming a C-instruction must include a jump; in fact jump bits can be all zeros for no jump. The compact dual-format design is deliberate: it separates immediate address loads from compute-and-store operations so assembly maps cleanly to machine words. Try encoding both types by hand to internalize the bit patterns.

The C-instruction’s three jump bits encode up to eight jump conditions that the C P U can test after computing an ALU result. The ALU provides two status flags: zr, which is true when the output equals zero, and ng, true when the output is negative. Using these two flags plus the three-bit jump field, the C P U implements conditions like JGT, JEQ, JGE, JLT, JNE, JLE, JMP, and no jump. For instance, JEQ fires when zr is true; JGT fires when neither zr nor ng is true, which indicates a positive result. JGE fires when not ng, covering zero or positive. JLE uses ng or zr to capture negative or zero. JMP unconditionally loads PC from A. The implementation is small: a combinational circuit checks the jump bits against zr and ng and produces a signal to load the PC. A misconception is thinking the ALU must perform separate compare instructions; in Hack, every ALU operation naturally yields zr and ng as side effects, and the jump logic reuses them. When writing assembly, pick the comp that produces the value to be tested, then set the jump bits to the condition you want. How would you implement a 'jump if not equal' using the ALU flags?

Let’s walk through a concrete program that adds 2 and 3 and stores the sum in R A M[0]. The assembly uses six instructions that load constants and perform computation. We start with @2 which sets A to two. Next D=A copies that value into D. Then @3 sets A to three. D=D+A instructs the ALU to add D and A, placing five into D. Then @0 sets A to zero, and M=D stores D into R A M[0]. Translating these to machine code: @2 becomes 0 followed by 15-bit binary for 2. D=A is a C-instruction that sets dest to D and comp to A, similarly encoded. When you manually translate, produce each 16-bit word and verify that the A-instructions start with 0. During execution trace the registers: after @2 and D=A D holds 2. After @3 and D=D+A D holds 5. After @0 and M=D R A M[0] holds 5. A useful check is to ensure you didn’t accidentally overwrite D when changing A. Also confirm that only the C-instruction M=D writes to R A M. This example reveals how a few instructions manipulate A, D, and memory to perform simple arithmetic and storage.

The chapter suggests three hands-on programs to solidify your understanding: swapping two values using a temporary, a countdown that stores intermediate values, and finding the maximum of two values using conditional jumps. For swap, the plan is simple: load R A M[0] into D, store D into R A M[2] as temporary, load R A M[1] into D, write it to R A M[0], then restore R A M[1] from R A M[2]. For countdown, initialize R A M[0] with 10, then loop: store the current value into the next R A M slot, decrement the counter, and jump when not zero. This exercise trains stack-like memory usage and loop control using jump bits. For find max, load R A M[0] and R A M[1], compute their difference into the ALU, and use jump bits to decide which value to store into R A M[2]. Each program requires you to produce both assembly and the corresponding 16-bit binary words. When translating by hand, encode each A-instruction as 0+value and encode each C-instruction by selecting a, comp, dest, and jump fields. A common debugging approach is to step through the PC and record A, D, and R A M snapshots after each instruction to confirm correctness. These exercises force you to manage A carefully, choose dest bits, and use jumps. Which program will you implement first?

Here are the core ideas to take with you. First, the programmer-visible registers are A and D; M is a shorthand for R A M[A], so A plays a dual role as value and address. Second, the memory map divides writable R A M (0–16383), a memory-mapped screen (16384–24575), and the keyboard at 24576. Third, instruction memory (ROM) is separate and read-only; the PC steps through ROM and jumps load PC from A. Fourth, there are exactly two instruction formats: A-instructions load A with a 15-bit value and begin with 0; C-instructions begin with 111 and include a, comp, dest, and jump fields. Fifth, comp bits drive the ALU, and dest bits choose where the ALU output is stored. Sixth, jump bits use the ALU’s zr and ng flags to express conditional branching. These compact mechanisms show how a small instruction set and a minimal register file can still express useful computation and control flow. Keep these relationships in mind when translating assembly to binary and when tracing programs.

Keep three compact reminders handy. First: A is address-or-value, D is the data workspace, and M always means R A M[A]. Second: A-instructions start with 0 and load A with a 15-bit immediate; C-instructions start with 111 and encode computation, destinations, and optional jumps. Third: Jumps are implemented by the three jump bits combined with the ALU flags zr and ng; no separate comparator hardware is needed. These three reminders let you spot encoding errors, reason about loops, and predict the effect of each instruction on registers and memory. When you hand-encode and trace programs, start by deciding whether an instruction is an A- or C-instruction, then fill in comp, dest, and jump for C-instructions, or write the immediate bits for A-instructions. That small workflow will make translating and debugging predictable and fast.
